bollymeter.basis: 95% on Rotten Tomatoes from 195 critics. Colin Farrell's transformation and Cristin Milioti's scene-stealing Sofia Falcone gave critics what amounted to a character study wrapped in a mob drama - darker and more precise than superhero TV typically manages.

pull_quotes.text: A ferociously entertaining crime drama elevated by two powerhouse lead performances - and Colin Farrell is unrecognisable in the best possible way.

seasons.review_body: The Penguin is the best argument DC has made in years for the superhero-adjacent limited series format. Lauren LeFranc built eight episodes around Oz Cobb's ascent - and crucially, the show works as a crime drama first and a DC property second. Colin Farrell under three hours of prosthetics delivers a performance of genuine menace and dark comedy, but the critical surprise was Cristin Milioti as Sofia Falcone: wounded, brilliant, and terrifying. Critics pointed to the show's willingness to let Gotham be genuinely grimy - no CGI spectacle, mostly intimate rooms and bad decisions. The 5.3 million viewers at launch were the highest-rated HBO premiere in two years, and the critical score (95% RT) put it among the best DC productions ever made.

episode_reviews.title: After Hours
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Penguin picks up immediately after the Riddler's flooding of Gotham in The Batman (2022), dropping Oz Cobb into the power vacuum with nothing but audacity and tactical instinct. The premiere establishes the series' register - Sopranos-adjacent mob drama with superhero-adjacent origin story - and confirms that Colin Farrell's prosthetic transformation is matched by a performance of comparable depth.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Oz Cobb surveying a flooded, ruined Gotham and calculating exactly how to turn catastrophe into opportunity - the moment that defines the character for the entire run.
episode_reviews.review_body: The Penguin's premiere operates as a thesis statement: this is not a superhero series but a crime drama that happens to occupy a superhero-adjacent world. Set in the immediate aftermath of The Batman's Riddler flooding Gotham, the episode drops Oz Cobb into a power vacuum and watches him work. Colin Farrell's physical transformation via prosthetics is extraordinary, but the performance underneath it is the real achievement - Oz is calculating, resentful, and genuinely funny in ways that make him compelling even at his most brutal. At 95% on Rotten Tomatoes from 195 critics, the series earned that response largely from how the premiere established its tonal commitment. The decision to frame a Batman universe spinoff as a Sopranos-inflected character study proved immediately effective in the opening episode.

episode_reviews.title: Sofia in Wonderland
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Episode 3 is The Penguin's formal statement of ambition: a Sofia Falcone backstory episode that operates as a standalone psychological portrait. Cristin Milioti's performance is the episode's whole argument - what happens to a woman whose patrician family processes her as a liability. The episode reframes the entire season.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Sofia's account of Arkham - the specific, calm way she describes what happened to her there - the scene that makes the entire season's power dynamic suddenly legible.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# The Penguin S01E03: "Sofia in Wonderland" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The election news comes first. Bella Reál is leading Acting Mayor Tomlin, City Hall is waiting for fireworks, and the roof looks like the safest place to watch Gotham pretend it still has ceremonies. Then the skating story turns fatal, Calvin’s name cuts through the scene, and bombs appear everywhere. Everyone gets down. That is the episode’s argument in miniature: every plan in this hour starts as a pitch and ends as a survival drill. "Sofia in Wonderland" works best when it treats crime as logistics under pressure, with Victor as the kid learning that pressure has a way of choosing for you.

## The Fireworks Become a Warning

The opening run is smart because it starts outside the drug trade. It starts with public power. Bella Reál leading Tomlin on election night gives Gotham a civic backdrop, while the plan to watch fireworks from a roof lends the scene a false normality. The city is voting, people are moving upstairs, and for a minute the danger has the shape of weather in the distance.

Then Calvin’s name lands. The fatal skating-story thread and the call of “Calvin!” put private missing-person panic beside the public spectacle. The episode does not need to explain the entire emotional bill in that moment. It only needs to connect Calvin to disappearance and alarm, and it does. The bombs that follow turn loose social movement into immediate panic.

That abrupt switch is the hour’s favorite rhythm. Calm, pitch, rupture. It can be blunt, but here the bluntness has function. Gotham does not let any room stay one kind of room for long. A roof becomes a danger zone. A night of politics becomes cover for chaos. A name shouted in fear becomes an open loop the hour refuses to close.

That refusal matters. Calvin’s disappearance does not get neatly parked. It lingers as a question while the drug plot takes over, and that gives the episode a useful unease. The city is exploding in the background, but the smaller absence cuts sharper.

## Bliss Is a Business Plan Before It Is a Temptation

When **Oz** is introduced to Trey Bloom, the episode shifts from panic to process. Trey is cooking up the components, and the new product gets its name: Bliss. That naming beat is clean. A crime story often asks the drug itself to carry too much atmosphere, but this hour cares more about how a product becomes an operation. Ingredients, pitch, price, distribution. The ugliness is in the spreadsheet.

That is where the episode finds its snap. Bliss is not treated as a vague magic powder. It is positioned as a distinct high, then moved into a sales strategy. By the time the party pitch begins at 20 a hit, the episode has already walked from invention to branding to street test. The momentum is commercial, not mystical. Gotham’s underworld does not sit around admiring evil. It packages it.

Oz fits that machinery because he understands movement. His problem is baked into the plan. He wants the trade to work under the new drug arrangement, but the hour keeps pushing him into questions of betrayal and counter-betrayal. That is a good Oz engine: ambition with a knife tucked inside it. He does not merely sell Bliss. He has to sell confidence while everyone around him is measuring the distance to his back.

The episode occasionally trusts the density of talk more than the shape of a scene. The dialogue momentum is relentless after longer transition silences, and some beats need more air. Still, the business spine carries the hour. Bliss enters as a product, then exposes the people trying to control it.

## Victor Chooses the Trap He Wanted to Leave

**Victor** gives the episode its most human contradiction. He wants out. The pull toward California gives him a future that does not have to be Gotham-shaped. Then the hour puts him in the exact role that makes escape harder: bagman for Bliss sales at the club.

That turn works because it is practical. Victor is not dragged into a grand symbolic ritual. He is given a job. Money moves through his hands. The new drug plan needs bodies, trust, and someone willing to stand close enough to the transaction to get blamed if it breaks. That is the trap. Crime does not always recruit through speeches. Sometimes it hands over a bag and calls it responsibility.

The party sales pitch sharpens that idea. Bliss is being introduced as something new, the price is set, and Victor becomes part of the product’s first real circulation. The pressure comes from the mismatch between what he wants and what he is doing. He wants distance. His task demands proximity.

This is the hour’s best character work because it does not overstate Victor’s fall. It stages one compromise and lets the compromise breathe. He is not suddenly transformed into Oz. He is still a person with an exit sign in his head. The episode understands that the first step into a life can look like helping someone else’s plan succeed for one night.

The final declaration that he and Oz are “in it now” lands because the hour has earned the phrase operationally. It is a status update.

## Sofia Sells Trust in a Room Built to Doubt Her

**Sofia Falcone** has the episode’s title gravity, and her business problem is brutal: she needs trust. Bliss requires approval, support, and buyers who believe the operation will not collapse under the weight of its own history. Feng Zhao’s concerns about her past and Arkham history put the challenge in the open. Sofia is selling a future to people still reading her through the institution that tried to define her.

That is a loaded position, and the episode is strongest when it keeps the tension transactional. Sofia does not need a grand confession. She needs men with money and leverage to accept her as the person steering the next move. That makes the Bliss plan larger than Oz’s hustle. It becomes a test of whether Sofia can convert stigma into authority.

**Johnny Viti** complicates that balance from inside the power structure. His interest in leverage, the coup plan, and calling out Oz while backing restructuring and support claims makes him the kind of ally who sounds useful until the invoice arrives. The hour uses him well as a pressure point. Every claim of support feels like it carries a second purpose.

This is where "Sofia in Wonderland" earns its title without becoming abstract. Sofia’s wonderland is a room where every smile has terms and every objection has history behind it. Zhao’s doubt gives the hour a hard business obstacle. Viti gives it internal rot. Oz gives it velocity. Sofia has to turn all of that into trust before the operation eats itself.

## The Attack Makes the Pitch Honest

The end interruption works because it punctures the sales fantasy at the correct moment. The episode spends its middle stretch building Bliss into a plan: cook it, name it, price it, move it through the club. Then violence intrudes and strips the plan down to its real cost. After the attack, Victor and Oz declaring they are in it now admits what the characters have been trying to outrun.

This is the episode’s best structural move. It makes the party pitch feel like a setup without reducing it to setup. The sales reps, Vic as bagman, the price point, the new-drug confidence, all of it matters because the attack lands on a working machine. If the plan were vague, the chaos would be noise. Because the plan has mechanics, the chaos has impact.

The limitation is clarity of emotional focus. Calvin’s disappearance, Oz’s betrayal anxieties, Sofia’s approval problem, Viti’s maneuvering, Zhao’s doubts, and Victor’s escape conflict all move at once. The hour runs hot. The density gives the episode charge, but a few transitions sprint past reaction. The show wants urgency, and it gets it. It also leaves some feeling on the table.

Still, the ending pulls the threads into one blunt truth. Nobody gets to keep the fantasy version of the night. The city loses its fireworks. Oz loses his clean rollout. Sofia loses her frictionless business pitch. Victor loses the comfort of California glowing somewhere offscreen. The attack makes the pitch honest.

## The Verdict

"Sofia in Wonderland" is a strong, busy hour built around one sharp idea: plans in Gotham are only real after they survive interruption. The episode moves from election-night spectacle to bomb panic, from Trey Bloom’s drug components to Bliss as a priced product, from Victor’s escape dream to his role as bagman, and from Sofia’s trust pitch to a room full of doubts. Its weakness is overcrowding. Some scenes push so much dialogue and maneuvering forward that reaction gets squeezed. But the hour’s structure holds. Bliss is introduced as commerce, then tested by violence, and Victor’s final position beside Oz gives the season a cleaner moral bind than any speech could. BollyAI's score: 8.1.

verdict.one_liner: Bliss gives the hour its engine, but Victor’s trapped loyalty gives it the bruise that lasts.

episode_reviews.title: A Great or Little Thing
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Penguin's finale resolves the mob war it has been building since the premiere and delivers on Oz Cobb's coronation as the series' title character in both name and power. A satisfying close that earns its darkness without exploiting it, and leaves Gotham's gangland in a configuration the broader DC universe will have to reckon with.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Oz's final act against the Falcone family - the specific, precise nature of his vengeance, which makes his transformation into the Penguin feel inevitable rather than scripted.
episode_reviews.review_body: The finale of The Penguin delivers on the mob drama the series established in episode 1. Oz Cobb's arc from opportunistic lieutenant to crime lord completes itself here with a specificity the DC universe rarely achieves in its origin stories. The violence of the climax is earned rather than spectacular - the series has done the character work to make the Penguin's emergence feel inevitable. Sofia Falcone's arc reaches its conclusion in a way that maintains the co-protagonist structure that distinguished the series from a straightforward villain spinoff. At 95% RT and 8.2 IMDb, the finale contributes to a limited series that holds up as DC's best-executed character study in the streaming era.
